meta.title: Benchmarked, Rarely Field-Tested: Computer Vision for End-of-Life Product Data in Industrial Ecology
meta.subtitle: A taxonomy of CV applications, mapped to physical scale and information type
meta.source: van Lierde et al., "Benchmarked, Rarely Field-Tested: Computer Vision for End-of-Life Product Data in Industrial Ecology" (review article) [citation: forthcoming], Table S2 (per-task descriptors). Verdicts are the article's; do not alter without changing the article.

maturityLevels.gloss: Tested well enough to use within its stated limits.
maturityLevels.handling: Accept the value and record where it came from.

maturityLevels.gloss: A method exists. It needs adjustment or human checks, or works less well in a different setting.
maturityLevels.handling: A person checks each value. Record the extra uncertainty and note that it came from a field photo.

maturityLevels.gloss: Shown to work for one type of object. Performance on other product types is not established.
maturityLevels.handling: For products in general, a person must supply the value. Do not fill an inventory entry from this result.

maturityLevels.gloss: The idea has been demonstrated in principle or in a related field. There is no systematic test of its performance on these products, so performance in practice is unknown.
maturityLevels.handling: A person enters the value and checks it in more than one way. Do not use a camera estimate for the inventory.

maturityLevels.gloss: There is no direct method for this task. The answer may need to be calculated from other information.
maturityLevels.handling: Work the value out from other sources.

product.name: End-of-life desk fan
product.note: Representative multi-component WEEE product chosen for the visualization. The taxonomy is product-general: its axes are physical scale and information type, and the evidence behind the verdicts spans washing machines, laptops, smartphones and vehicles. The paper's Table S3 and Figure S1 walk this same desk fan through three disassembly stages.

cells.task: Identify the product and read its label details
cells.methodFamily: Reading the label's text (OCR) and matching it to a database; matching the photo against reference images (retrieval, one-shot recognition)
cells.maturityNote: The method is in use, but labels become harder to read as products move toward recycling. Software read model numbers from 95.7% of images with a visible label at repair, 90.8% at reuse and 39.7% at recycler intake. Both the study of this drop and the collection-site pilot come from one research group. Independent confirmation is still missing.
cells.hardware: Photos are taken on the device; recognition is better run on a server.
cells.failureMode: End-of-life labels are damaged, dirty, skewed or too far away. The database may not cover the product. It is not automatic: a person picks the final match.
cells.example: Washing-machine label reading on phone and tablet cameras (Sterkens et al. 2023). Identifying the exact model of discarded devices in an instrumented sorting cell (fixed cameras and sensors): 90.3% right on the first guess across 1,958 models of undamaged devices (Koyanaka & Kobayashi 2024). A six-camera rig at a take-back facility matched worn appliances by waste category, not by model: 93.6% accuracy and 88.4% mAP@5, the precision of the top five matches (C. Zhou et al. 2025). Pilots at an e-waste sampling center and a distribution center read the model number from 51.5% and 69.5% of legible label images, and 18% of sampled devices had no label (Sterkens & Peeters 2024).

cells.methodFamily: Depth from one photo (monocular metric depth); 3D shape from several photos (feed-forward multi-view geometry). A 3D model generated from one photo is for documentation only.
cells.maturityNote: Software can estimate shape and distance from photos. Tests cover general scenes; measurements of products have been demonstrated but not systematically tested. Weight is estimated too: about one estimate in four is off by more than a factor of two. A generated 3D model is not a measurement.
cells.hardware: Depth from one photo can run on the phone; several photos or generated 3D are better on a server.
cells.failureMode: Only visible surfaces count. Scale still depends on the camera details stored with the photo. Weight adds the error in shape to the error in material.
cells.example: Weight from a single photo (Standley et al. 2017; Lee et al. 2026; Wang et al. 2026). Geometry evidence: depth from one photo (Hu et al. 2024, Metric3D v2; Bochkovskii et al. 2025, Depth Pro; Yang et al. 2024, Depth Anything V2; R. Wang et al. 2025, MoGe-2). 3D from several photos (J. Wang et al. 2025, VGGT; Keetha et al. 2025, MapAnything). Phone depth sensing (Luetzenburg et al. 2021; Hamilton-Fletcher et al. 2024).

cells.maturityNote: Connections are assessed at the parts level (Component · Structure). This cell has no separate task or rating, and no row in Table S2. Its evidence mark is –.

cells.task: Judge wear and damage, to decide between repair, reuse and recycling
cells.methodFamily: Detecting known defects with trained models; flagging unusual areas without examples (zero-shot anomaly detection: WinCLIP / AnomalyCLIP); describing the product in words (vision-language models, VLMs). Triage in use today sorts by value or material.
cells.maturityNote: Condition grading has been tested for one type of product at a time, using fixed camera rigs. Software graded laptop covers A to E with 86.7% accuracy across the full process on previously unseen models. Another study graded the severity of damage to smartphone screens. Researchers ran both systems. Both are sensitive to lighting, and neither has been tested on field photos.
cells.hardware: Could run on a phone in principle; the tested systems are tied to a fixed rig.
cells.failureMode: Not tested on field photos, and known to be sensitive to lighting. Works for one product class only. Triage in use today still sorts by value or material.
cells.example: Laptop-cover grading from A to E on an instrumented rig, 86.7% end-to-end (Wu et al. 2026). Smartphone screens graded by severity (Mohandas et al. 2025). Kiosk device grading, a narrow class with instrumented capture (Bowles et al. 2012; Li & Huang 2021). Exterior vehicle damage assessment (Hasan et al. 2025) remains the closest example from a neighbouring field. An industry grading scale for phones and tablets sets defect levels in millimeters (CTIA Certification 2019).

cells.task: Identify each part and read its markings
cells.methodFamily: Reading text (OCR); finding and naming parts from a typed description (open-vocabulary detection); matching against reference images (retrieval)
cells.maturityNote: Software can name parts, but struggles to tell very similar parts apart. Performance is weak outside the settings it was trained on: 15.7 mAP, a score out of 100 for finding objects, across a range of settings.
cells.hardware: Photos are taken on the device; recognition is better run on a server.
cells.failureMode: Markings may be missing or worn. Software that has not been trained for this task performs poorly on unfamiliar kinds of image.
cells.example: Reading component markings, as at product scale (Sterkens et al. 2023). Naming parts from a typed description (Liu et al. 2025, Grounding DINO). Weak zero-shot results across many domains, 15.7 mAP (Popov et al. 2025). Battery type read from markings in photos from a battery-sorting facility, precision 0.98 and recall 0.67 for packs of 300 g or more (0.88 and 0.54 below) (Sterkens et al. 2022). That last study is context only: it names a battery type group, not a part, and has no clean-photo comparison.

cells.task: Measure each part's size, weight and shape
cells.methodFamily: Depth from one photo (monocular metric depth); 3D shape from several photos (feed-forward multi-view geometry)
cells.maturityNote: The same methods estimate size, shape and weight for individual parts as for whole products. They share the same limits.
cells.hardware: Phone or server, as for the whole product.
cells.failureMode: Parts hide each other inside an assembly, so even less surface is visible. Scale is still sensitive to the camera.
cells.example: Depth from one or several photos (Hu et al. 2024, Metric3D v2; Wang et al. 2025, VGGT).

cells.task: Find, outline and count the parts, and how they attach (Bill of Components)
cells.methodFamily: Detecting parts from a fixed or an open list; outlining any region with a large pretrained (foundation) model, then labelling it; for attachments, inferring joints from an image (image-to-articulation)
cells.maturityNote: Finding and outlining parts is rated Partial. One narrow test reports ~98.8% mAP50, a score for finding objects, but the software needs adjustment for each setting. Outlines learned at one waste-sorting facility score 56.0 mIoU, a measure of overlap with the correct outlines, and 45.5 at another. Identifying how parts attach is Emerging-but-narrow: methods cover only jointed household objects or toy vehicles. In one study of jointed household objects, the whole connection map was correct in ~82% of cases on one dataset and ~39% on an unseen dataset. This tests generalisation, not performance on repair-shop photos. The rating for finding and outlining parts rests on one lab-photographed teardown study.
cells.hardware: Fixed-list detection can run on the phone; open-vocabulary and foundation models need a server.
cells.failureMode: Performance drops outside the setting used for training. The software needs adjustment to that setting and a way to name each outlined part. There is no general method for mapping how parts attach.
cells.example: Segmenting parts in e-waste and laptop teardowns (Zhang et al. 2026). Waste segmentation tested across facilities (Bashkirova et al. 2023). Foundation segmentation that also labels what it outlines (Carion et al. 2025, SAM 3). Joints inferred from an image (Liu 2025 SINGAPO; Chen 2024 URDFormer; Yuan 2025 LARM).

cells.task: Judge wear, damage and connector state, to decide what happens to each part
cells.methodFamily: Detecting known defects with trained models; connector state (requirements level, graded per unit only on lab-corroded screws); robots driven by vision-language-action models (embodied/VLA, immature)
cells.maturityNote: There is no system for grading the condition of connectors on products. Researchers have described what such a system would need to check. Grading individual screws has only been shown on screws corroded in a lab and mounted on test plates. Demonstrations rely on a central robot station.
cells.hardware: Tied to servers and robotic cells, where it has been shown.
cells.failureMode: Grading individual connectors has not been validated outside a central facility. Robot disassembly of this kind is unreliable: 0 of 20 full operations finished without help.
cells.example: Robotic disassembly cells (Liu et al. 2026, RAISE; Liu et al. 2025, VLA selective disassembly). Connector-state evidence: requirements level (Saenz et al. 2024). Rust grading on lab-corroded screws on test plates (Mandolini et al. 2026). Vision-guided screw removal that completed disassembly on 72 of 92 in-scope air-conditioner units (Ishikura et al. 2026). Fastener and screw detection for disassembly with a collaborative robot (Sutradhar et al. 2025).

cells.task: Identify materials on and under the surface (Bill of Materials)
cells.methodFamily: Classifying colour photos under controlled conditions (RGB classification); matching against one or a few examples, given an outline of the region; few-shot vision-language models; outlining material regions across a surface
cells.maturityNote: Software identifies materials on visible surfaces under controlled conditions. The review found no method for measuring the composition of hidden interiors, coatings or alloys. The only related trial used a photo-based sorter on shredded electronic waste (Vogelgesang et al. 2025). That trial describes mixed fragments from unidentified products. It does not identify the materials in one intact product, so it does not meet the requirement for use on individual products.
cells.rubricMarks: B · ✗ᵃ · ✗ (close-adjacent benchmark: in-the-wild material appearance, not EoL products)
cells.hardware: Lightweight classifiers can run on the phone; vision-language recognisers need a server.
cells.failureMode: Objects made of several materials are hard to label: ~90% on TrashNet falls to ~40% on MultiWaste. Performance also drops when the setting changes. In an extreme example, an older system using colour photos fell from 100% to ~12–28% overall under two hand-held lighting changes, with 0% on up to 3 of 4 classes. A third run, on a robot arm at 77 lx, kept ~78%. Clutter in realistic scenes also hurts.
cells.example: Material recognition by a vision-language model without examples (Funk et al. 2026). Colour-photo material classification under controlled conditions (Penumuru et al. 2020). Outlining materials across 3D surfaces (Li 2024 MaterialSeg3D; Drehwald 2023). A component-level bill of masses from circuit-board photos, tested on four off-the-shelf boards (Chedotel et al. 2026).

cells.methodFamily: Worked out from other cells: part geometry times material class times a typical density
cells.maturityNote: There is no direct method. Material mass must be calculated from estimated shape, material type and density. Errors in shape and material identification both affect the result. The paper uses – for this evidence mark because the answer is calculated from other results.
cells.hardware: Depends on the tools used to estimate shape and identify materials.
cells.failureMode: Errors from both inputs add up. Image-to-mass methods are tested only on off-the-shelf circuit boards, whole catalog objects, and discarded packaging and food photographed by calibrated smart-bin cameras.
cells.example: Derived from other cells; no direct method.

cells.maturityNote: Connections are assessed at the parts level (Component · Structure). This cell has no separate task or rating, and no row in Table S2. Its evidence mark is –.

cells.methodFamily: Outlining surface regions; monitoring particle size (only in known streams)
cells.maturityNote: The idea is plausible, but has not been tested for products in general.
cells.hardware: A phone or server, depending on the method used to outline material regions.
cells.failureMode: A change of setting or a cluttered scene reduces performance. No validated method grades the condition of each material region.
cells.example: Surface segmentation (Li et al. 2024, MaterialSeg3D); particle segmentation for size monitoring of crushed aggregates, on simulated images (Y. Zhou et al. 2025, ParticleSAM).
